post.contentHtml:
Japanese candy maker Kanro (カンロ, Tokyo Stock Exchange: 2216) makes sweets such as its signature "Kanro Candy," jelly, and gummies. Its share price has fallen about 33% over the past year, yet around 30% of the company is held by Mitsubishi Corporation, one of Japan's largest trading houses. This article looks at both sides of the story: the reasons behind the share price decline and the sturdy major shareholder.

Where the Stock Stands Now

ItemDetails
Recent share priceAbout ¥1,057 (data as of November 13). The November 9 closing price was confirmed at ¥1,022, so the stock appears to have traded in the low-to-mid ¥1,000 range in mid-November.
1-year price changeAbout -33%
Annual dividend¥32 (¥8 per quarter). Dividend yield of about 3.0% based on ¥1,057
Median annual trading valueAbout ¥110 million. This is not a heavily traded stock, so liquidity needs to be checked.

* The exact closing price as of today could not be confirmed. The price above is the most recent value available, so please check again on your brokerage screen before trading.

Why the Stock Weakened: Sales Are Up, but Profit Is Down

In the first half of this year (January–June), Kanro's sales were about ¥17.46 billion and operating profit was about ¥2.15 billion. In the second quarter (April–June) alone, sales rose about 2.6% year on year, but net profit fell about 36%. In other words, sales volume held up while the money left over shrank.

  • Higher raw material and fuel costs: The cost of ingredients such as sugar, and of energy, went up.
  • Upfront hiring: The company added staff ahead of the launch of a new gummy production line, so labor costs rose first.
  • Reliance on one-off gains: First-half net profit includes a gain of about ¥150 million from selling shares it held. This should be viewed separately from the strength of the core business.

For reference, last year's (fiscal year ended December 2025) sales were about ¥34.77 billion and operating profit was about ¥4.69 billion. The company's profit forecast for this year is reported to be lower than that, but figures differ between sources, so it is safest to confirm the exact guidance in the company's disclosures.

The Most Interesting Point: Mitsubishi Corp. at 29.71%

At the top of the major shareholder list is Mitsubishi Corporation (29.71%). Below it come Enomoto Buhei Shoten (6.30%), Kanro Kyoeikai (5.59%, which appears to be a group of business partners and related parties), Sumitomo Mitsui DS Asset Management (3.72%), and the BNP Paribas Japan Small Cap Fund (2.49%).

  • A structure in which one holder owns about 30% also means few shares are available for trading. This ties in with the small trading value.
  • With such a influential major shareholder, management stability may be high, but this is only an estimate. How the major shareholder will act going forward has not been confirmed.
  • The ownership percentages reported at the end of September and the start of October are identical, so no major recent change in the shareholder makeup is visible.

Shareholder Returns: Share Buyback and Cancellation

According to what can be confirmed through searches, Kanro completed the share buyback it announced in July this year. It covered about 1.1 million shares (about 2.6% of shares issued) for roughly ¥1.2 billion, and the cancellation of treasury shares was reportedly completed at the end of August. The fact that the company bought back its own shares after the price fell offers a clue to how it views the current price. However, this does not guarantee a rebound in the share price.

What to Watch Next

  • Effect of the new gummy line: Labor costs have risen first, so the key is whether sales and profit margins actually improve once the line is running.
  • Whether cost pressure eases: Raw material and fuel prices need to stabilize before a margin recovery can be expected.
  • Next earnings release: Full-year results are reportedly due in early 2027. The schedule should be confirmed through company disclosures.
  • Dividend sustainability: Watch whether the ¥32 annual dividend is maintained while profit is shrinking. The record date for the year-end dividend is approaching in late December.

Summary

Kanro has two faces: a small food company whose share price has weakened under profit pressure, and a company with a stable shareholder structure in which a major trading house holds 30%. The share price drop from a year ago can be explained by rising costs and falling profit, but whether the new capital investment pays off will likely shape how the stock is valued from here. The low trading volume is also something investors should weigh.
